summary:
Lunar Site Navigator is a browser app that lets anyone pick a spot on the Moon and a date, and see where the Sun and Earth stand over the real terrain horizon. It answers the two questions that decide a south polar mission: will the solar arrays get light, and can the lander talk directly to Earth?

We built a 3D Moon from NASA LRO data (LOLA elevation, down to 80 m per pixel at the south pole, and the LROC colour mosaic) and compute the 360-degree horizon at any site from that terrain. Sun and Earth positions match NASA/JPL Horizons within 0.006 degrees. The app shows sunlight and Earth visibility hour by hour and finds landing dates that meet a mission's needs. It also works the other way round: say how much sunlight and Earth link a mission needs, over a year or chosen dates, and every south polar spot that fits lights up on the 3D Moon. It compares sites, estimates solar power and puts NASA Moon Trek's sunlight map and an orbital photo next to our own figure.

A built-in assistant, LUNA, gives a guided tour and plain-language briefings, so planners, teachers and students need no training.
details:
What it does

Lunar Site Navigator answers two questions for any point on the Moon and any date: is the Sun above the local horizon (power), and is the Earth above it (direct-to-Earth radio)? Near the south pole the Sun and Earth sit only a few degrees up, so a ridge 20 km away can switch a lander off or cut its link. The app shows this on real terrain, hour by hour.

  • 3D Moon from NASA data. LOLA elevation and the LROC colour mosaic, with the south polar cap built from the LOLA 80 m/pixel map. Shadows are traced toward the Sun, including the soft edge of the solar disc.
  • Pick a site from Apollo, Artemis III candidate regions and robotic landers, type coordinates, or click anywhere on the Moon.
  • Sun and Earth readouts: elevation, azimuth, the terrain horizon in that direction, how much of each disc clears the ridge, and a countdown to the next sunset or Earthset.
  • Horizon panorama: the 360-degree skyline around the site with the Sun's and Earth's paths over the month.
  • Lunar-month timeline: sunlight and Earth visibility hour by hour. Drag to scrub, step by a day or a month, or play.
  • Compare up to four sites and landing dates side by side: sunlight, solar energy, Earth visibility, both together, longest night.
  • Mission windows: enter a mission's length, sunlight and link needs, and see every landing date in the next year that works.
  • Find a site for a mission: the reverse of mission windows. Say whether a mission needs at least or at most a given share of sunlight and of direct link to Earth, on average over a year or over chosen dates (or a single landing day), add slope and ice limits, and the app checks up to 200 spots across the south polar cap against the real terrain horizon. Every spot that fits lights up on the 3D Moon, and a click flies there.
  • Power estimate: panel type, area, efficiency, load and battery give watts, the month's energy and whether the battery survives the night.
  • Stand on the surface: a first-person view at the site, with the Sun and Earth where they really are.
  • NASA Moon Trek, live: at the pole the site panel shows NASA's LROC sunlight map beside our own figure, plus a zoomable LROC photo of the spot from orbit.
  • Take it with you: a one-page PDF, an hourly CSV, and a link that reopens the same site, date and comparison.
  • LUNA, the mission assistant: a guided tour, plain-language site briefings, one-click rankings and a short mission game.

How accurate it is

Sun and Earth positions come from Astronomy Engine (VSOP87 / ELP) and the IAU lunar rotation model. We checked them against NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441): the largest error is 0.006 degrees over two years at four sites. The horizon is computed for 720 directions, marching up to 300 km outward over the LOLA terrain with the Moon's curvature included. A built-in "How accurate is this?" panel recomputes a year of sunlight at well-studied south polar sites and compares it with published LOLA results, and the site panel compares our figure with NASA's LROC map live.

Benefits and impact

Existing tools for this need specialist training. Here a mission planner can compare candidate sites and dates in minutes, a teacher can show a class why the Moon's south pole is so hard to land on, and anyone can see Artemis landing regions on real data. Everything runs in the browser with nothing to install, works offline once loaded, and adapts to the device: full effects on strong hardware, lighter settings on a weak laptop, and a flat relief map where 3D is not available. It opens in English and switches to Russian.

Tools and technology

TypeScript, React, three.js with React Three Fiber, custom GLSL shaders, Zustand, Vite and Vitest; Python with NumPy for preparing the NASA terrain and colour data; hosted on GitHub Pages. Source code: https://github.com/pythonhack000/lunar-navigator

What makes it creative

Every number is computed from true terrain and true ephemerides, not looked up from a table, so any point and any date work, not just a fixed list. The relief can be exaggerated for the eye without changing any result. And instead of a manual, LUNA walks new users through the interface on the live Moon. Most tools answer "is this site lit on this date?". Ours also answers the planner's real question the other way round: "where at the south pole can this mission land?", checking up to 200 spots against the real horizon and lighting the answers up on the 3D Moon.
